questions.question: What does receiving a message from SQS prove?
options: The business operation completed successfully
The message was permanently removed from the queue
The consumer holds a temporary receipt lease through the visibility timeout
No other delivery of that message can ever occur
questions.explanation: Receive makes the message temporarily invisible and returns a receipt handle. Completion requires the consumer's durable work and a successful delete with the current receipt handle.

questions.question: A workload requires updates to remain ordered per account, but different accounts may run concurrently. What is the best SQS design?
options: One Standard queue and send timestamps as the order
One FIFO queue with the account ID as MessageGroupId
One FIFO queue with the same MessageGroupId for every account
A separate queue for every individual message
questions.explanation: FIFO ordering is scoped to a message group. Grouping by account preserves each account's sequence while allowing unrelated accounts to be processed in parallel.

questions.question: Messages arrive at 800 per second. Consumers sustain 1,000 per second. After a 10-minute outage, how long does catch-up take while traffic continues?
options: 10 minutes
20 minutes
30 minutes
40 minutes
questions.explanation: The outage creates 800 x 600 = 480,000 queued messages. Spare capacity is 1,000 - 800 = 200 messages/second, so recovery needs 2,400 seconds, or 40 minutes.

questions.question: A handler takes 75 seconds but visibility is 30 seconds and is never extended. What is the main risk?
options: SQS deletes the message at 30 seconds
Another consumer can receive the message while the first is still working
The message moves directly to the DLQ after 30 seconds
The producer must resend the message manually
questions.explanation: When visibility expires, the undeleted message can be delivered again even though the first handler is still running. A measured timeout or visibility heartbeat reduces overlap, while idempotency protects the effect.

questions.question: A payment commits, then the worker crashes before DeleteMessage. Which boundary makes the retry safe?
options: A longer queue retention period
A larger receive batch
An idempotency record committed atomically with the payment
A second Standard queue
questions.explanation: SQS cannot atomically delete alongside an external payment store. The destination must recognize the same operation ID and ensure repeated delivery does not repeat the payment.

questions.question: Why can adding FIFO workers fail to increase throughput?
options: FIFO queues allow only one worker for the entire queue
Active parallelism is limited by available MessageGroupIds
FIFO consumers cannot use long polling
Every FIFO message must wait for the 14-day retention period
questions.explanation: Messages within one group remain ordered and are processed serially. More workers help only when enough independent message groups are available for concurrent ownership.

questions.question: What is the safest response to a permanently incompatible message schema?
options: Retry forever with no delay
Delete it without retaining diagnostic context
Quarantine after a bounded receive count, fix the cause, then redrive deliberately
Increase the visibility timeout to 12 hours
questions.explanation: A deterministic schema failure does not heal through retries. A bounded DLQ path preserves evidence and protects healthy work while operators repair and control the replay.

questions.question: Which metric most directly represents the user-visible freshness risk of an SQS backlog?
options: The number of queues in the AWS account
Approximate age of the oldest message
The configured maximum message size
The number of IAM policies
questions.explanation: Depth depends on job cost and arrival shape, while oldest-message age directly estimates how stale the next useful business effect can become.
